questions.question: What is the difference between == for primitives vs == for objects in Java?
questions.title: == for Primitives vs Objects in Java
questions.direct_answer: For **primitives**, `==` compares the actual **values** directly. For **objects**, `==` compares **references** (memory addresses) — it checks whether both variables point to the same object, not whether the objects have equal content. This split is one of the most common sources of bugs in Java.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's value vs reference semantics — the foundational distinction that affects every data structure decision
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using == to compare String or Integer values and being confused when identical-looking values return false
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the Integer cache (-128 to 127) as a gotcha where == sometimes works for objects, making the bug even harder to spot

sections.title: Value Comparison vs Reference Comparison
sections.content:
The `==` operator has two different behaviors depending on what you compare. For **primitives** (`int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char`), `==` compares the actual values — it checks if the numbers or characters are identical. For **objects** (`String`, `Integer`, custom classes), `==` compares **references** — the memory addresses where the objects live. Two variables can point to objects with identical content but different memory locations, so `==` returns `false` even though they look the same.

Comparing house addresses: for primitives, `==` checks if the house numbers match; for objects, `==` checks if two people are standing in the exact same house, not whether their houses look similar. That is why you see `userName.equals(otherName)` instead of `userName == otherName`.

sections.title: == on Primitives vs Objects at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|== on primitives|~Compares values|5 == 5 is true|works for int/double/char|no method needed
blue|== on objects|~Compares references|same object in memory|content is ignored|two equal-looking objects are false
emerald|.equals()|~Compares content|the safe choice|override in custom classes|use for String/Integer
rose|Integer cache|~-128 to 127 reused|== true in range|== false at 128+|always use equals for wrappers

sections.title: Primitives vs Objects with ==
sections.content:
| Aspect | Primitives (`int`, `double`, `boolean`) | Objects (`String`, `Integer`, custom) |
|---|---|---|
| What `==` compares | Actual values in memory | Memory addresses (references) |
| When `==` is `true` | Values are mathematically equal | Both variables point to same object |
| Typical use case | Numeric comparisons, boolean checks | Identity checks, null checks |
| For content equality | Use `==` directly | Must use `.equals()` |
| Example `true` case | `int a=5, b=5; a==b` | `String s2 = s1; s1==s2` |

sections.title: Wrong — == on Integer objects looks fine until it isn't
Right — compare wrapper values with equals()
sections.content:
```java
Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x.equals(y));                     // true — compares value
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.equals(x, y)); // true — and null-safe
```
For objects, reach for `.equals()` (or `Objects.equals` when nulls are possible), never `==`.

sections.title: When to Use Each Comparison Approach
sections.content:
Use `==` for **primitives** — it's the only way to compare `int`, `double`, `boolean`, `char` values.

Use `==` for **objects only when checking identity or null**: `if (user == null)` or `if (currentUser == loggedInUser)` where you specifically need the exact same instance.

Use **`.equals()`** for object content comparison — checking if two strings have the same characters, if two `Integer` wrappers hold the same number, or if two custom objects are logically equivalent. In a login system, use `userName.equals(inputName)`, never `userName == inputName`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **String comparison with `==`**: `if (userName == "admin")` sometimes works (string interning) but breaks when the string comes from user input or a file — an intermittent bug.
- **Ignoring the Integer cache**: `Integer x = 100; Integer y = 100; x == y` is `true`, but at `200` it's `false`. `==` seems to work for `Integer` until values exceed 127.
- **Confusing equals() direction**: `userName.equals("admin")` throws `NullPointerException` if `userName` is null; use `"admin".equals(userName)` or `Objects.equals(...)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Primitives** — `==` compares values directly; `5 == 5` is `true`, no method needed.
- **Objects** — `==` compares memory addresses; two separate `"hello"` objects return `false`.
- **Identity vs equality** — `==` checks same object; `.equals()` checks same content.
- **Null safety** — `x == null` is safe; `x.equals(y)` crashes if `x` is null.
- **Integer cache** — `-128` to `127` are cached, so `==` works in range but fails outside.
- **Best practice** — never use `==` for `String`, `Integer`, or custom objects unless you need reference equality.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The difference is that for primitives, double equals compares the actual values, but for objects, it compares references, basically memory addresses. So if you have two int variables with value 5, double equals returns true because the values match. But if you have two String variables both containing the word hello, double equals usually returns false because they're separate objects in memory, even though the content is identical. That's why we use the equals method for objects, it actually looks at the content. The tricky part is that sometimes double equals seems to work for objects, like with String literals, because Java interns them into a shared pool. But the moment you read a string from user input or a file, you get a new object and double equals breaks. There's also the Integer cache. Java caches Integer objects from negative 128 to 127, so double equals works in that range but fails at 128 and above. I've debugged this exact bug before when code worked in testing with small numbers but failed in production. The rule I follow is, use double equals only for primitives and null checks. For any object content comparison, always use equals, or better yet, Objects dot equals if there's any chance of null values.

questions.question: What is the difference between if-else if-else chain and switch statement for multiple conditions?
questions.title: if-else Chain vs switch Statement — When to Use Each
questions.direct_answer: **if-else if** chains evaluate sequentially and support any boolean expression including ranges and complex conditions. **switch** jumps directly to the matching case (more efficient for many discrete values) but only supports equality checks. For 5+ discrete value checks, `switch` is more readable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Code design judgment — knowing when each construct is appropriate shows practical experience beyond syntax
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using long if-else chains for discrete values that would be cleaner as a switch, or trying to use switch for range checks
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention switch expressions (Java 14+) that return values and eliminate break statements, making switch even more attractive for discrete values

sections.title: Sequential Evaluation vs Direct Jump
sections.content:
**if-else if chains** evaluate conditions top to bottom, stopping at the first `true`. They support any **boolean expression** — range checks (`age > 18`), complex logic (`status.equals("ACTIVE") && balance > 0`), method calls, null checks. They're flexible but get hard to read with many branches.

**switch statements** perform a direct jump to the matching case, making them efficient for checking one variable against many discrete values. Traditional `switch` only works with equality on `int`, `char`, `String`, `enum` — no ranges. Java 14+ **switch expressions** return values directly with arrow syntax, eliminating `break` and fall-through bugs.

The practical rule: use `if-else` for ranges or complex conditions; use `switch` for 5+ discrete values of one variable (status codes, enum states, command parsing).

sections.title: if-else vs switch at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|if-else if|~Sequential top-down|any boolean expression|ranges and complex logic|checks multiple variables
blue|switch|~Direct jump|equality checks only|int/char/String/enum|jump table, fast
emerald|switch expression|~Java 14+ arrows|returns a value|no break needed|no fall-through
rose|Pick by case count|~2-4 use if-else|5+ discrete use switch|enums prefer switch|always add default

sections.title: if-else if vs switch
sections.content:
| Aspect | if-else if chain | switch statement |
|---|---|---|
| Condition types | Any boolean expression | Equality checks only |
| Supports ranges | Yes (`age >= 18 && age < 65`) | No (must enumerate values) |
| Multiple variables | Yes | No (single switch variable) |
| Performance | Sequential, O(n) worst case | Jump table, O(1) typical |
| Readability (many cases) | Verbose, hard to scan | Clear, tabular |
| Fall-through | N/A | Needs `break` (or arrow syntax) |

sections.title: Wrong — missing break causes fall-through
Right — switch expression has no break and no fall-through
switch Expression with Enums (common real-world use)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **if-else if** for range checks (`age` between 18 and 65), conditions across multiple variables, complex boolean logic (null checks, AND/OR combinations), or fewer than about 5 discrete cases.

Use **switch** for one variable checked against 5+ discrete values (order status, day of week, HTTP codes), for enums (the compiler enforces exhaustive handling), or when performance matters with many cases. In modern Java 17 projects, prefer switch expressions — concise, value-returning, and free of fall-through bugs.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Missing `break` in traditional switch**: causes fall-through where multiple cases run — the #1 switch bug.
- **Using switch for ranges**: `case 0-17:` is invalid; ranges require `if-else`.
- **Over-using if-else for discrete values**: 10 `else if` branches for status codes that a `switch` would document clearly.
- **No default case**: omitting `default` makes code brittle when new values appear — always handle the unexpected case.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **if-else flexibility** — any boolean expression, ranges, multiple variables.
- **switch efficiency** — direct jump, O(1) for many discrete values.
- **switch limits** — equality only, on `int`, `char`, `String`, `enum`.
- **switch expressions** — Java 14+, return values, no `break`, no fall-through.
- **Threshold** — `if-else` for 2-4 conditions; `switch` for 5+ discrete values.
- **Default** — always include a `default` to handle unexpected values.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The main difference is flexibility versus efficiency. if-else if chains are super flexible. You can check any boolean condition, like age greater than 18, or status equals active and balance over 1000, or even call methods. They evaluate sequentially from top to bottom, stopping at the first true condition. But with many branches, they get hard to read and slower since every condition is checked in order. switch statements are more restricted. They only work for checking one variable against multiple discrete values, like comparing order status to pending, confirmed, or shipped. But they're more efficient because the JVM can jump directly to the matching case using a jump table. They're also more readable when you have five or more cases, it's like a lookup table. The traditional gotcha with switch is forgetting the break statement, which causes fall-through bugs. But modern Java from version 14 onward has switch expressions with arrow syntax that return values directly and don't need break, much cleaner. In practice, I'd use if-else for ranges or complex conditions, and switch for discrete values like enums or status codes. If you're working with enums, switch is definitely the way to go because the compiler can check that you've handled all possible values.

questions.question: What is the difference between while and do-while loops — when would you use do-while?
questions.title: while vs do-while Loop — Real Use Cases
questions.direct_answer: **while** checks the condition before executing — it may execute zero times. **do-while** checks the condition after — it guarantees at least one execution. Use `do-while` when the loop body must run once unconditionally, like showing a menu or reading initial input before validating.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding when do-while is the right tool — not just syntax knowledge but practical design judgment
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Forgetting the semicolon after the while condition in do-while: } while (condition);
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give a concrete scenario where do-while is the natural choice — input validation, menu-driven programs, retry logic with a guaranteed first attempt

sections.title: Pre-Check vs Post-Check Loops
sections.content:
**while loops** evaluate the condition before each iteration, including the first. If the condition is false initially, the body never runs — zero iterations. **do-while loops** execute the body first, then check the condition, guaranteeing at least one iteration.

The key difference is timing: `while` is a **pre-check loop** (test, then maybe do), `do-while` is a **post-check loop** (do, then test if you should repeat).

`while` is "check if you should enter the store, then enter"; `do-while` is "enter the store, then check if you want to stay." In real code `do-while` is rare (maybe 5% of loops), but it fits perfectly for menus, reading data where at least one read is required, and retry logic that always tries once.

sections.title: while vs do-while at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|while|~Pre-check loop|test then maybe run|zero iterations possible|about 90% of loops
blue|do-while|~Post-check loop|run then test|at least one iteration|about 5% of loops
emerald|Use do-while|~Run once for sure|menu programs|input validation|retry with first attempt
rose|Syntax gotcha|~Semicolon needed|} while (cond);|missing it is an error|easy to forget

sections.title: while vs do-while
sections.content:
| Aspect | while | do-while |
|---|---|---|
| Condition check | Before each iteration (pre-check) | After each iteration (post-check) |
| Minimum iterations | Zero (may never execute) | One (always runs once) |
| Typical use | Unknown count, may skip entirely | Must run once, then repeat conditionally |
| Syntax gotcha | No semicolon after condition | Semicolon required: `} while (cond);` |
| Frequency | Very common (90%+) | Rare (~5%) |

sections.title: Awkward — dummy value just to force the first run
Natural — do-while guarantees the first prompt
Menu-Driven Program (classic do-while case)
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **while** for almost all loops — iterating collections, reading files until EOF, polling until a condition changes. It's the default because most loops should be skippable if the condition is false from the start.

Use **do-while** in three scenarios: (1) **menu-driven programs** that must show the menu at least once, (2) **input validation** that prompts at least once and repeats until valid, (3) **retry logic** that always attempts once before checking whether to retry. If you find yourself initializing a variable just to make the `while` condition true the first time, that's a smell — use `do-while`.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Forgetting the semicolon**: `} while (condition)` without `;` is a compile error specific to do-while.
- **Using do-while when while is clearer**: forcing one iteration where the logic doesn't require it confuses readers.
- **Accidental infinite do-while**: forgetting to update the control variable — it runs once and then loops forever, less obvious than a while that never starts.
- **Skipping pre-validation**: do-while always runs the first iteration; if you need to validate before running, do-while is wrong.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **while** — condition checked before body; may run zero times; most common.
- **do-while** — condition checked after body; always runs at least once.
- **Syntax** — do-while needs a semicolon: `} while (condition);`.
- **Menu pattern** — do-while suits menus that must display before checking the choice.
- **Input validation** — do-while naturally says "prompt, then validate, repeat if invalid."
- **Smell** — initializing dummy values to force `while` once means you want `do-while`.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The key difference is when the condition gets checked. while checks the condition before running the loop body, so if the condition is false from the start, the loop never executes, you get zero iterations. do-while flips that around. It runs the loop body first, then checks the condition afterward, which means you're guaranteed at least one iteration no matter what. The classic example is a menu-driven program. With do-while, you show the menu at least once, then check if the user chose exit. If you used while, you'd have to initialize the choice variable to something that makes the condition true just to get the menu to display the first time, which is awkward. Input validation is another good use case, you want to prompt the user at least once, then keep prompting if the input is invalid. Or retry logic where you always try the operation once before deciding whether to retry. In practice, do-while is pretty rare, maybe five percent of loops in real code, but when you need guaranteed first execution, it's the cleanest solution. The one syntax gotcha is that do-while needs a semicolon after the while condition. Freshers always forget that and get a compile error. If you find yourself setting up dummy values just to force a while loop to run once, that's a sign you should be using do-while instead.

questions.question: What is the difference between Comparable and Comparator in Java?
questions.title: Comparable vs Comparator in Java
questions.direct_answer: **Comparable** defines the **natural ordering** of a class — implemented inside the class with `compareTo()`. **Comparator** defines an **external, custom ordering** — a separate class or lambda comparing two objects. Use `Comparable` for the default sort; use `Comparator` for alternate sorts or when you can't modify the class.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Java's sorting mechanism and when to use each interface — demonstrates collections framework knowledge
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they're interchangeable, or not knowing Comparable is one method in the class itself while Comparator is a separate strategy
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Show modern Java 8+ Comparator syntax with lambdas and method references like Comparator.comparing(User::getName)

sections.title: Natural Ordering vs Custom Ordering
sections.content:
**Comparable** is an interface you implement inside a class to define its **natural ordering** — the default sort. You implement one method, `compareTo(T other)`, returning negative, zero, or positive. `Collections.sort(list)` on `Comparable` objects uses this built-in logic.

**Comparator** is a separate interface defining custom ordering outside the class — a strategy you create (often a lambda) that compares two objects. Use it when you need multiple sort orders (users by name, then by age), when you can't modify the class (sorting built-in types), or when sorting logic doesn't belong in the domain object.

Think of `Comparable` as the class saying "here's my default order" and `Comparator` as you saying "sort these this specific way right now."

sections.title: Comparable vs Comparator at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Comparable|~Natural ordering|defined inside the class|int compareTo(T o)|one ordering per class
blue|Comparator|~Custom ordering|external lambda or class|int compare(a, b)|unlimited orderings
emerald|Java 8 style|~Concise lambdas|Comparator.comparing|thenComparing chains|reversed() flips
rose|Pitfall|~compareTo of 0|must agree with equals|avoid a minus b overflow|use Integer.compare

sections.title: Comparable vs Comparator
sections.content:
| Aspect | Comparable | Comparator |
|---|---|---|
| Where defined | Inside the class being compared | External class or lambda |
| Method | `int compareTo(T other)` | `int compare(T o1, T o2)` |
| Orderings | One natural ordering per class | Unlimited custom orderings |
| Modify class? | Yes, class implements interface | No, can sort any class |
| Example | `Collections.sort(users)` | `users.sort(Comparator.comparing(User::age))` |

sections.title: Comparable and Comparator in Practice
Wrong — subtraction in a comparator can overflow
sections.content:
```java
// Subtraction overflows for large or opposite-sign values
Comparator<User> byAge = (a, b) -> a.age() - b.age(); // overflow risk
```

sections.title: Right — Integer.compare is overflow-safe
When to Use Each
sections.content:
Use **Comparable** when there's an obvious default order — Orders by date, Employees by id, Products by name. Implement it once; `Collections.sort()` and `sorted()` work without extra parameters.

Use **Comparator** when you need multiple sort orders, when sorting by criteria not central to the object, when you can't modify the class (`LocalDate`, `String`), or when sorting depends on external data. Modern Java 8+ makes `Comparator` so concise with lambdas that many teams use it even where `Comparable` would do.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Returning 0 incorrectly in compareTo**: returning `0` when objects differ breaks `TreeSet`/`TreeMap`, which discard "duplicates."
- **Inconsistent with equals**: if `compareTo` returns `0`, `equals` should return `true`; violating this breaks sorted collections.
- **Subtraction for ints**: `this.age - other.age` overflows with opposite signs; use `Integer.compare(...)`.
- **Not handling nulls**: comparator lambdas crash on null fields; use `Comparator.nullsFirst(...)`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Comparable** — one natural ordering inside the class via `compareTo`.
- **Comparator** — unlimited external orderings via `compare`.
- **compareTo contract** — negative if less, zero if equal, positive if greater.
- **Comparator.comparing** — Java 8 factory taking a key extractor like `User::getName`.
- **Chaining** — `thenComparing` for multi-level sorts, `reversed()` to flip.
- **Modern preference** — `Comparator` with lambdas is the most flexible in real code.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Comparable and Comparator both let you sort objects, but they work differently. Comparable is something you implement inside the class itself. You write a compareTo method that defines the natural, default ordering for that type. So if you have a User class and you implement Comparable, you're saying by default users should be sorted by name, or whatever makes sense. Then you can just call Collections dot sort and it works automatically. Comparator, on the other hand, is external. It's a separate piece of logic that compares two objects. You use it when you need a different sort order than the default, or when you need multiple ways to sort the same class, or when you can't modify the class. For example, you might sort users by name in one place and by age in another. With Java 8 and lambdas, Comparator became really concise. You can write things like Comparator dot comparing User get name, which is one line and super readable. You can even chain them with thenComparing for complex sorts. One trap is using subtraction inside a comparator, like a minus b, which can overflow. Use Integer dot compare instead. In my experience, Comparator with lambdas is more common in real code because it keeps sorting logic separate and flexible, but Comparable is great when there's an obvious default order everyone agrees on.

questions.question: What is the Integer cache in Java and how does it affect == comparisons?
questions.title: Integer Cache in Java — The -128 to 127 Gotcha
questions.direct_answer: Java **caches Integer objects for values -128 to 127**. When you autobox an int in this range, Java returns the same cached `Integer` object instead of creating a new one. So `==` returns `true` for two `Integer` variables with values in this range but `false` outside it — a classic interview trap.

interviewer_intent.testing: Awareness of Java's object pooling optimization and how it affects reference equality — separates candidates with real debugging experience
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Expecting == to work consistently for all Integer values, not understanding why it breaks at 128
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the rationale behind -128 to 127 (most common int values, performance for autoboxing) and always recommend equals() for Integer comparison

sections.title: Integer Object Pooling and Autoboxing
sections.content:
The **Integer cache** is a performance optimization where Java pre-creates and reuses `Integer` objects for values from -128 to 127. When you write `Integer x = 100` (autoboxing), the JVM doesn't create a new object — it returns a reference to the cached object for 100.

So two variables holding 100 point to the same object and `==` is `true`. But `Integer x = 200; Integer y = 200;` creates two separate objects, so `==` is `false` even though both hold 200. This is a **classic trap** because code seems to work in testing (small numbers) but breaks in production with larger values. The cache exists because small integers are extremely common — loop counters, indices, status codes. The lesson: **never use `==` to compare `Integer` objects** — use `.equals()`.

sections.title: Integer Cache at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|Integer cache|~-128 to 127 reused|autobox returns cached|saves memory|common small ints
blue|In range|~== works|Integer 100 == 100 is true|same object|deceptive
emerald|Out of range|~== breaks|Integer 200 == 200 is false|new objects|bug in production
rose|Other types|~Also cached|Byte Short Long -128..127|Character 0..127|always use equals

sections.title: Integer Cache Behavior
Wrong — relying on == for Integer passes only by luck
Right — equals() compares value regardless of cache
sections.content:
```java
Integer x = 200, y = 200;
System.out.println(x.equals(y));                     // true
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.equals(x, y)); // true — null-safe too
```
The -128 to 127 range is guaranteed by the spec, but its upper bound is configurable via `-XX:AutoBoxCacheMax`, so never depend on `==`.

sections.title: How to Safely Compare Integer Objects
sections.content:
Always use **`.equals()`** to compare `Integer` values — it works regardless of cache range.

Use **`Objects.equals(a, b)`** for null-safe comparison when either value might be null.

Use `==` only for null checks: `if (userId == null)`. You can rely on the cache to save memory with small integers, but never write logic that depends on `==` behavior — it's an optimization detail.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Testing only with small numbers**: `==` comparison passes with `1, 2, 5` thanks to the cache, then production fails with larger IDs.
- **Confusion at the boundary**: `Integer.valueOf(100) == Integer.valueOf(100)` is `true` but at `200` it's `false`; this looks like broken autoboxing.
- **Assuming the cache is fixed**: the upper bound is configurable via a JVM flag — defensive code never relies on `==`.
- **Mixing primitives and wrappers**: `Integer x = 200; int y = 200; x == y` unboxes and is `true`, while two `Integer` 200s are `false`.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache range** — Java pre-creates `Integer` objects for -128 to 127.
- **== split** — `true` for cached values, `false` outside, revealing the bug.
- **Rationale** — small integers are extremely common; caching saves memory.
- **Other cached types** — `Byte`, `Short`, `Long` (-128 to 127), `Character` (0 to 127).
- **Safe comparison** — always use `.equals()` for `Integer`, never `==`.
- **valueOf vs new** — `Integer.valueOf(n)` uses the cache; `new Integer(n)` bypasses it (and is deprecated).

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The Integer cache is a performance optimization in Java where the JVM pre-creates and reuses Integer objects for values from negative 128 to 127. So when you autobox an int in that range, like Integer x equals 100, you don't get a new object, you get a reference to a cached one. This means if you have two Integer variables both set to 100, they actually point to the same object, so double equals returns true. But here's the trap. If you do the same thing with 200, Java creates two separate objects, so double equals returns false even though both hold 200. I've seen this bug in production. Code works fine during testing with small numbers, then mysteriously breaks when real data has larger IDs or counts. The reason Java does this is that small integers are super common in programs, loop counters, array indices, HTTP status codes. Caching them saves memory and speeds up autoboxing. The cache range is guaranteed by the Java spec, but the upper bound can actually be configured with a JVM flag. The lesson is, never use double equals to compare Integer objects. Always use equals, or even better, Objects dot equals if there's any chance of nulls. It's one of those gotchas that makes Java interviews tricky but also reflects a real-world bug pattern you need to watch for.

questions.question: What is the difference between String comparison using == vs equals() vs compareTo() in Java?
questions.title: String == vs equals() vs compareTo() in Java
questions.direct_answer: **`==`** compares references (never use for string content). **`.equals()`** compares string content (case-sensitive, returns `boolean`). **`.compareTo()`** compares lexicographically (returns a negative/zero/positive `int`, used for sorting). For content equality, always use `.equals()`.

interviewer_intent.testing: Complete understanding of string comparison methods — this is fundamental Java knowledge tested in nearly every interview
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the return value semantics of compareTo() (negative means before, zero means equal, positive means after)
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention Objects.equals(a, b) for null-safe comparison and equalsIgnoreCase() for case-insensitive checks

sections.title: Three Ways to Compare Strings
sections.content:
String comparison in Java has three methods, each for a different purpose. **`==` compares references** — it checks if two variables point to the same `String` object, not whether the characters match. Because of interning, `==` sometimes appears to work with literals but breaks with runtime strings. **`.equals()` compares content** — character by character, case-sensitive; this is what you use for ~95% of equality checks.

**`.compareTo()` compares lexicographically** — it returns an `int`: negative if the first string comes before, zero if equal, positive if after. It's used for sorting and `Comparable`. Three questions: `==` asks "same object?", `equals` asks "same text?", `compareTo` asks "which comes first alphabetically?" Never use `==` for string content in production.

sections.title: String Comparison at a Glance
sections.content:
amber|==|~Reference identity|same object?|null checks only|never for content
blue|.equals()|~Content equality|same text? (case-sensitive)|returns boolean|the 95% choice
emerald|.compareTo()|~Lexicographic order|which comes first?|returns int negative/zero/positive|used for sorting
rose|Helpers|~Null-safe and case|Objects.equals(a, b)|equalsIgnoreCase|compareToIgnoreCase

sections.title: String Comparison Methods
sections.content:
| Method | `==` | `.equals()` | `.compareTo()` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Compares | Memory references | Character content | Lexicographic order |
| Return type | `boolean` | `boolean` | `int` (neg/zero/pos) |
| Primary use | Null checks only | Content equality | Sorting, ordering |
| Case sensitivity | N/A | Yes (`equalsIgnoreCase`) | Yes (`compareToIgnoreCase`) |
| Meaning | same object | same content | neg=before, 0=equal, pos=after |

sections.title: Wrong — == on String content
Right — equals() for content, compareTo() for order
All Three Methods Together
sections.content:
```java
String name1 = "Alice", name2 = "Alice", name3 = new String("Alice"), name4 = "Bob";

System.out.println(name1 == name2);          // true  — interned literals
System.out.println(name1 == name3);          // false — new object
System.out.println(name1.equals(name3));     // true  — same content
System.out.println(name1.compareTo(name4));  // negative — "Alice" < "Bob"

String missing = null;
System.out.println(java.util.Objects.equals(name1, missing)); // false, no NPE
System.out.println(name1.equalsIgnoreCase("alice"));          // true
```

sections.title: When to Use Each Method
sections.content:
Use **`==`** only for **null checks**: `if (input == null)`. Never for content.

Use **`.equals()`** for content equality — login validation, comparing input to expected values.

Use **`Objects.equals(a, b)`** when either string might be null — no `NullPointerException`.

Use **`equalsIgnoreCase()`** for case-insensitive equality — emails, usernames.

Use **`.compareTo()`** for ordering — sorting names, implementing `Comparable` (`str1.compareTo(str2) < 0` means str1 comes first). In real projects `.equals()` is by far the most common.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Using `==` for content**: works with literals (interning) but fails with runtime strings — intermittent bugs.
- **Ignoring null with equals**: `userName.equals("admin")` crashes if `userName` is null; use `"admin".equals(userName)` or `Objects.equals(...)`.
- **Misreading compareTo**: thinking it returns `true/false`, or not knowing negative means "before."
- **Case assumption**: using `equals` where `equalsIgnoreCase` is needed (emails, usernames).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`==`** — checks same object; only use for null checks with strings.
- **`.equals()`** — character-by-character, case-sensitive; the standard equality method.
- **`.compareTo()`** — returns `int` (neg/zero/pos); used for sorting and `Comparable`.
- **Null safety** — `Objects.equals(a, b)` avoids NPE that `a.equals(b)` would throw.
- **Case variants** — `equalsIgnoreCase()` and `compareToIgnoreCase()`.
- **Best practice** — always use `.equals()` for content, never rely on `==` except for null.

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: There are three ways to compare strings in Java, each with a different purpose. First, double equals compares references. It checks if two variables point to the exact same object in memory, not whether the strings have the same content. You should never use double equals for string comparison except for null checks. The tricky part is that double equals sometimes seems to work because Java interns string literals into a shared pool, but the moment you read a string from user input or a database, you get a new object and double equals breaks. Second, equals compares content. It goes character by character and checks if two strings have identical text. This is case-sensitive and it's what you use ninety-five percent of the time. If either string might be null, use Objects dot equals instead to avoid a null pointer exception. Third, compareTo is for ordering. It returns an int that tells you alphabetical order. Negative means the first string comes before the second, zero means they're equal, and positive means it comes after. You use compareTo when sorting strings or implementing the Comparable interface. There are also case-insensitive variants like equalsIgnoreCase and compareToIgnoreCase for things like email addresses where case shouldn't matter. The bottom line is, always use equals for content equality, never double equals, and use compareTo only when you need ordering information for sorting.
